lead: RFID is a way to give a thing an electronic identity that a reader can capture without contact and without line of sight. A tag holds a code; a reader radios the code out; middleware passes it to a database. The code is the key, not the whole record. Used on toll tags, library books, access cards, shipping pallets and animal chips. This chapter explains the parts, the radio bands, passive and active tags, the EPC code, singulation and the privacy cost of hidden tags.
prereq: You need 2.4 for radio modules and power ideas.

sections.h3: Identity, parts and why a reader is needed

blocks.text: Identification in IoT means giving a thing a name or number that a computer can use as a database key. A key alone does nothing; the system must capture it. RFID has three parts. A tag is a chip plus an antenna, attached to the thing. A reader has a transmitter, a receiver and an antenna; it powers or wakes tags and receives their codes. Middleware cleans the stream: it removes duplicate reads, filters false reads and maps each code to a record in the server. The EPC is the code; the database holds price, batch, owner or location.

A barcode and a QR code are printed patterns read by light. They need line of sight, one label at a time, and they cannot be rewritten. An RFID tag is read by radio through cardboard or plastic, many tags can answer in one pass, and a read-write tag can be updated. The trade is cost: a printed label is cheap; a tag costs more.

The band decides range and behaviour. LF and HF use near-field inductive coupling: the reader coil makes a magnetic field, the tag coil takes power from it, and the tag changes its load to send bits. UHF and microwave use far-field backscatter: the reader radiates a wave, the tag harvests a little power, and it reflects the wave by switching its antenna load. Backscatter is why a passive UHF tag can be read several metres away without a battery.

A passive tag has no battery; it uses reader power. A semi-passive tag has a battery for its chip but still backscatters. An active tag has its own transmitter and can start a message; it costs more and needs battery care.

sections.h3: EPC Gen 2, singulation, other IDs, privacy

blocks.text: EPC Gen 2 is a UHF air-interface standard for passive tags. Its common EPC is 96 bits: an 8-bit header, a 28-bit manager number, a 24-bit object class and a 36-bit serial number. The reader must read one tag at a time even when many reply. EPC Gen 2 uses frame-slotted ALOHA with the Q parameter: the reader sets a frame of slots, and each tag picks a random slot so that most tags answer alone. Binary-tree splitting is a different anti-collision method used by some other UHF standards; it divides colliding tags into smaller groups until each answers alone. Both methods solve the same problem: many tags, one reader.

Other identifiers used with things: an IPv6 address names a network interface and works over the Internet; 6LoWPAN compresses IPv6 for IEEE 802.15.4 links; a BLE beacon broadcasts a short ID that a phone can hear. These are not RFID: they need a radio network or a phone, not a dedicated tag reader.
NFC is HF RFID at 13.56 MHz built into a phone. It works at a few centimetres: the phone can read a tag, act as a tag, or talk to another phone. Metro cards, door cards and tap-to-pair use it.

A hidden tag can be read after the buyer leaves the shop. A card in a pocket can be a people-tracking token. A kill command can disable a tag permanently; a blocker tag or shielded sleeve can stop reads. Privacy law is in Unit 5.

examples.question: A reader at 866 MHz radiates 2 W ERP. A passive tag needs 30 µW at its chip to wake up, and its antenna gain is 2 (about 3 dBi). Find the power reaching the tag at 3 m and the maximum read range in free space.
steps: ERP is referenced to a half-wave dipole, so first convert to EIRP: EIRP = 1.64 × 2 = 3.28 W.
With 3.28 W EIRP, at d = 3 m the power density is S = 3.28/(4π×3²) = 0.0290 W/m².
Tag effective aperture: A_e = Gλ²/(4π) = 2×0.346²/(4π) = 0.0191 m²; G = 2 is the tag antenna gain.
The tag needs P_min = 30 µW. In free space P falls as 1/d², so d_max/d = √(P/P_min) = √(554/30) = 4.30.
examples.answer: At 3 m the tag chip receives 554 µW, so with 30 µW needed the free-space read range is 12.9 m.
examples.check:
import math
f=866e6; c=3e8; ERP=2.0; G=2.0; Pmin=30e-6; d=3.0
EIRP=1.64*ERP
lam=c/f; Ae=G*lam**2/(4*math.pi); S=EIRP/(4*math.pi*d*d); P=S*Ae; dmax=d*math.sqrt(P/Pmin)
print(round(lam,3)); print(round(Ae,4)); print(round(S,4)); print(round(P*1e6,0)); print(round(dmax,1))

traps: A passive tag has no battery, so its read range is set by the forward power delivered to its chip, not by the backscatter return link.
NFC is HF RFID at 13.56 MHz, not UHF 860–960 MHz; do not put NFC in the toll-tag band.
EPC is an identifier code; EPC Gen 2 is a UHF air-interface standard. Do not call EPC a tag type.
A semi-passive tag has a battery but still backscatters; an active tag has its own transmitter and can start a message.
Keep units straight: ERP is not EIRP, W is not dBm, and cm is not m in range formulas.

quiz.q: What are the two hardware parts of a passive RFID tag?
quiz.a: A chip and an antenna; it has no battery.

quiz.q: Why can an RFID tag be read through a cardboard box while a barcode cannot?
quiz.a: RFID uses radio waves that pass through non-metal materials; a barcode needs visible light and line of sight.

quiz.q: A passive tag receives 120 µW at 2 m. What does it receive at 4 m in free space?
quiz.a: Power falls as 1/d². Distance doubles, so power becomes one quarter: 30 µW.

quiz.q: Why is the read range of a passive tag set by the forward link, not by the backscatter link?
quiz.a: The chip needs a minimum wake-up power from the reader. Once awake, the reflected signal usually has enough margin for the reader to decode.

quiz.q: Give one reason to choose QR over RFID and one reason to choose RFID over QR in a warehouse.
quiz.a: QR: printed labels are very cheap. RFID: reads many tags without line of sight and can rewrite the tag.

quiz.q: Which band does NFC use, and what is its typical range?

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry calls UHF Gen 2 RAIN RFID; EPCIS shares tag events across a supply chain. Research looks at chipless tags, printed antennas and backscatter radio that reuses ambient signals. Privacy work studies kill commands and blocker tags. Search: EPC Gen 2, EPCIS, RAIN RFID, chipless RFID.
